I'm visiting my sister, her husband, and my niece in the Northeastern US. It's been a bit rainy and balmy here and I thought pho would be great for dinner. There's a big Vietnamese community in New Orleans where I live, so buying ingredients down there is a simple matter of going to 1 store and picking up what I need. That wasn't the case here, but I was committed. After 3 stops I had found most if what I needed, but before starting to cook, I needed to clean up the kitchen...

Both my sister and BIL work and my niece is in kindergarten. They both leave the house early and get home around 5, at which time my sis exercises for about an hour and my BIL chills on the couch with my niece as she has her afternoon snack. I know they're busy so when I do get a chance to visit them, I like to spend my days working on house projects.

As I started putting food away from my grocery trip, I also began throwing away expired food from the pantry, rotting leftovers from the fridge, organizing the shelves, and taking a general inventory of what they had. When I was finished I had thrown away 3 full 13-gallon trash bags of junk. Some things I found included several bottles of salad dressing from as far back as 2014 with 1 or 2 tbsp left in them, literally 5 cans of baking powder that were all expired and barely used, boxes of cereal left unsealed each with only crumbs at the bottom, a total of 6 lbs rolled oats in 4 different containers of various brands all opened and in different cabinets -- you get the idea.

Most of what I did was consolidate and organize like items together (like all oatmeal and breakfast foodstuffs together on the same shelf, all snack foods in the snack drawer, etc.), throw away expired goods, and put open and unsealed things like bags of flour or opened seasoning packets into Ziploc bags to store them with like items.

Once I had finished that, I could finally clean the countertops and make my pho.

To make the broth I cook a whole chicken in a big pot with water, star of anise, allspice, fresh ginger shavings, fresh garlic and onion, and whatever vegetable ends/pieces I have lying around. Today I used mushroom stems, bok choy stems, the stems from the herbs I bought, and cooked that down all day. After about 3 hours I took the chicken out, picked the meat off of it, and threw the bones and fat and offal back into the pot to cook down for another few hours. The broth eventually gets strained and set aside. The finer the strainer the clearer the broth will be.

I precooked the rice noodles, seared some various veggies to add, diced chives and grated ginger, then made nam pla thai-style with the diced Thai chilis and sliced garlic. I cleaned the mint, basil, mung bean sprouts and cilantro and set that aside, then sliced lime and set up all the ingredients buffet style. I also have siracha, sesame oil and soy sauce available on my buffet line up.

In the end the soup was more of a pho/mohinga hybrid but it was a big hit.

My sister appreciated having the night off from cooking dinner, and couldn't believe how much crap had accumulated in her cabinets. Keeping your pantries and refrigerators organized is a great way to reduce food waste and therefore, money waste. It's also important for preventing pests from getting a foothold in your home -- I am amazed how many crumbs and nuts and chocolate chips and other filth I wiped out of those cabinets today.

Now that I know everything she has in her kitchen, I don't even need to go to the store tomorrow to make an awesome dinner for our parents who will be joining us.
